title: Deino Q3 board update

calendarEvent.title: Deino Q3 board update
calendarEvent.description:
Agenda:
1. Q3 metrics (Aisha)
2. Pipeline (Aisha)
3. Product and engineering, incl. Calendar Sync v1.4 incident (Shreyas)
4. Q4 priorities and SOC 2 (Shreyas)
5. For approval: two engineering hires
6. Fundraising timing

Board deck: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1qR7bZ3kX9vLmT2wYpN4sJ8hD6fA0cE5uG/edit

Join Zoom: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/84213377610?pwd=Qm9hcmRRMzIwMjY

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can you hear us okay? Aisha and I are in the same room on one laptop, so if it sounds like we're in a cave, that's why.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hi Daniel, we can see you. Ruth, I think you're still connecting.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I can hear you both fine. A little echoey, but fine. I'm in a phone booth at our office, so apologies if someone knocks on the glass.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Hello, hello. Sorry, I'm here now. I had you down as tentative because a client call was running into this, but I managed to move it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Thank you for moving it, Ruth. Sam sent his apologies, he's at a portfolio offsite this week, so it's just the four of us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yeah, Sam's in Lisbon at our annual thing. He'll read the deck, and he asked me to say he's sorry to miss it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Lisbon. Some of us are in a spare bedroom with a dog who wants a walk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: How's the new office, by the way? Aisha said you finally moved out of the coworking space.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's good. We have actual meeting rooms now, although the wifi in one of them is a disaster. That's where Aisha wanted to take this call, and I said absolutely not.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: He's not wrong. It dropped twice during an interview last week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What kind of dog is it, Ruth?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: A very old beagle called Biscuit. He'll be asleep in ten minutes, don't worry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, let's get going, I know everyone has a hard stop at the hour. The deck went out on Friday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The plan is I do the Q3 numbers and pipeline, Shreyas does product and engineering, including the Calendar Sync incident. Then we have two things we need you to decide, the two hires and fundraising timing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Sounds good to me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So, Q3. We're one day from the end of the quarter, so these are effectively final.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: ARR is two point four million, up from one point nine at the end of Q2. That's about twenty-six percent quarter on quarter.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We have forty-one paying customers, up from thirty-four. Gross margin is seventy-eight percent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Of the seven new logos, five are HVAC or plumbing, one is electrical, and one is a pool service company. All mid-market, no enterprise yet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Net revenue retention is one hundred and eighteen percent, which is down from one twenty-four last quarter. I'll come back to that, because I know Daniel will.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: You know me too well.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: On the cash side, monthly burn is about three hundred and ten thousand, cash in the bank is five point nine million, and that's about nineteen months of runway at the current burn, with no revenue growth assumed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Before you go on, what's gross retention? Net hides a lot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Gross revenue retention is ninety-four percent for the trailing twelve months. We lost one logo this quarter, which I'll explain in a minute, and the rest of the gross loss is seat contraction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Ninety-four is healthy for this segment. Okay, carry on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And that nineteen months is before the two hires you're asking for?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Before the hires, yes. I'll show you the after picture when we get there.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay. Can I start with burn efficiency, because I think that's the headline for me. You added about half a million of net new ARR this quarter, and you burned roughly nine hundred and thirty thousand to do it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's a burn multiple of about one point nine. It's better than Q2, I think Q2 was something like two point three, but it's not where I'd want a company at your stage going into a Series A.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Agreed, it's not where we want it either. Q2 was two point three, you're right. The trend is in the right direction, and I think we can get to one and a half by Q2 next year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What's actually in the three ten? Roughly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Roughly two hundred and forty thousand is payroll for the fourteen of us. Cloud is about thirty-eight thousand, and that's mostly sync. The rest is software, the office, and Lena's travel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What gets you there, though? Because the easy answer is grow faster, and that's not a plan.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Three things. One is that our new customers are getting bigger. The average new customer in Q3 had about fifty-five technicians, versus about thirty a year ago, and the sales cycle hasn't gotten much longer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And CAC payback? Lena is still your only AE, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Lena is still the only AE, and I'm effectively the second one. Payback on Q3 deals is about fourteen months on a gross margin basis. That's okay, not great.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fourteen is fine for annual contracts. Don't hire a second AE until Lena's actually saturated, though. I've seen that go badly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We're not planning to before Q1. Maybe we revisit it in January, depending on Brightkite.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Two is gross margin, which Shreyas can talk to, because a big chunk of our hosting cost is calendar polling. And three, we're not growing headcount outside engineering for the next two quarters, except possibly a customer success hire.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On the margin point, today we poll every technician's calendar every five minutes. That's the single biggest line on our cloud bill.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Calendar Sync v2 moves us to webhook push, and our estimate is that it cuts sync compute by around sixty percent. That alone should take gross margin from seventy-eight to somewhere around eighty-one or eighty-two.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And it's a better product, because changes show up in seconds instead of up to five minutes later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Have you looked at committed-use discounts with your cloud provider? That's usually another few points of margin.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We've looked at it. Maybe after v2, once we know what the steady-state usage actually is. Committing now would mean committing to the polling bill.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Is support in your cost of revenue? Because Tom's time has presumably gone up a lot this month.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yes, support is in COGS, so the incident shows up there too, a little. It's not a big enough number to move margin by a full point, but it's there.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay. When does v2 land?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Beta on the thirteenth of November, and general availability on the fourth of December. Maya Chen is leading it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: How far along is it, realistically?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The webhook ingestion is built and running against our own calendars. What's left is the Microsoft side, which renews subscriptions every few days and is fiddly, plus load testing and the migration from polling, customer by customer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fine. Now the NRR, because one twenty-four to one eighteen in one quarter is a meaningful drop. Is that a blip, or is something changing in the base?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think it's mostly a blip, but I'll give you the pieces so you can judge for yourself. There are three of them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The biggest is a pool and spa service customer in the southwest who cut twenty-five seats in August. They're seasonal, they lay technicians off after the summer, and they did exactly the same thing last year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The second is one small customer, eight technicians, who churned because they were acquired and the acquirer uses something else. And the third, which I'm less happy about, is Fernhollow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fernhollow is the HVAC company?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: HVAC and plumbing, about sixty technicians. They'd verbally agreed to add fifteen seats for a new plumbing crew in September, and that expansion slipped out of the quarter after they got hit by the calendar sync bug.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Owen, their operations manager, understandably wanted to see it fixed before he spent more money with us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So if the expansion had closed, where would NRR be?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Around one twenty-one. So still a dip, but a smaller one. And the seasonal customer, I expect them to add seats back in the spring, like they did this year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Is Fernhollow at risk? Not the expansion, I mean the account itself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'll be honest, they were frustrated, and they had every right to be. I don't think they're at risk of churning today, but it's not a relationship I'd call healthy right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Tom and I have a call with Owen next Monday to walk through the fix and the cleanup.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: What do you want to get out of that call with Owen?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Mostly to listen. Then show him the fix, the cleanup plan, and what we're changing so it doesn't happen again. The expansion only comes up if he raises it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Good. Let's come back to that in your section, then.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, pipeline. The one that matters most for Q4 is Brightkite Logistics. They have about two hundred and twenty field technicians and fourteen dispatchers across three regions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They're on spreadsheets plus an old on-prem tool called DispatchPro 6, and that licence ends on the thirty-first of January. So they have a real deadline, which we like.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They'd be on the enterprise tier because they need SSO, so at sixty dollars a technician that's roughly a hundred and fifty-eight thousand of ARR. Lena is running it, and the discovery call is tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: How did they find you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Their VP Operations, Marcus Webb, saw Lena's talk at a field service conference in the spring and kept our card. When the licence renewal quote came in, he called her.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: How real is it? Discovery is early.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's early. The deadline is real, and their VP Operations reached out to us, not the other way around. But I'd put it at maybe thirty percent today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Their IT security lead is joining the call tomorrow, which tells me they're serious. It also tells me they're going to ask about SOC 2.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And pricing? Two hundred and twenty seats is going to come with a discount ask.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It will. Our floor is fifty-four, which is ten percent off list, and only for a multi-year term. I'd rather lose a little on price than set a precedent below that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Good. Hold that line. The first big logo always tries to reprice you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then there are three other enterprise deals. An elevator maintenance company with about a hundred and twenty technicians, which is at proposal stage, and a regional pest control company with about ninety, which is in security review.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And a facilities group with about three hundred technicians, which is very early and honestly a long shot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: When does the elevator one close?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We're hoping for mid-November. They've seen the proposal, and the main open point is SSO, which we already have on the enterprise tier, so I'm reasonably optimistic.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And the pest control one, what's holding up the security review?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They asked for a SOC 2 report, which we don't have yet. Priya sent them our security overview and the pen test summary from June, and they're deciding whether that's enough for now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: So that's a deal that SOC 2 directly unblocks. Worth remembering when you're tempted to deprioritise it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Who are you up against in these? Is it the big incumbents, or other startups?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Mostly the big incumbents, the all-in-one field service suites. They win on breadth, we win on the dispatch board and the calendar sync. Customers who mainly care about scheduling pick us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Honestly, in two of the four enterprise deals the real competitor is doing nothing and renewing what they have.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's usually the hardest one to beat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: What's the plan for Q4 new ARR?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The plan is six hundred thousand of net new ARR, which gets us to about three million exiting the year. That's without Brightkite. Brightkite would be upside.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What's your pipeline coverage against that six hundred?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: About two and a half times, excluding Brightkite. Lena's forecast is more conservative than mine, which is probably healthy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And Q4 NRR? Do you expect it to recover?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If the Fernhollow expansion closes in Q4, and I think it will once the fix is out, we should be back above one twenty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Okay. Then let me ask the concentration question, because enterprise deals change your shape. What's your largest customer as a share of ARR today?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Our largest customer is nine percent of ARR. That's the regional utilities contractor, about three hundred technicians on the enterprise tier, on a three-year contract that renews in 2028.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The top five together are thirty-one percent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Nine percent is fine, I start to worry above fifteen. But if Brightkite and the elevator company both close, your top five will be close to forty percent, and they'll all be the same kind of customer with the same kind of demands.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The thing I've seen go wrong is that the enterprise accounts start setting the roadmap, and the mid-market customers who actually got you here get quietly neglected.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's a fair warning. Honestly, it's part of why we cut the Salesforce integration from Q4. One enterprise prospect asked for it, and it would have eaten a whole quarter.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And who looks after those accounts once they've signed? You have a support engineer, but as far as I can tell you don't have customer success.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We don't. Tom Becker is our support engineer, Lena does some account management, and I do a lot of it myself, which doesn't scale. We'd pencilled in a customer success hire for Q1.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I'd think about doing it sooner. And I know someone who'd make a great VP of Customer Success.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: She ran customer success at a field service software company that was acquired last year, and she's looking. I'll introduce you to her.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That would be great, thank you. I'll gladly take the intro.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Before we move on, is a VP really the right level for a company with forty-one customers? It feels heavy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Maybe it's a head of rather than a VP, I'm not precious about the title. She's very hands-on. Aisha can decide after meeting her.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And Aisha, honestly, the other reason I'd do it sooner is you. You're the CEO, the second AE, the customer success team and, from March, the fundraiser. Something gives.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I know. It's mostly the customer success part that keeps me up at night. Fine, I'll meet her and keep an open mind on timing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Agreed on the title question too. Okay, Shreyas, over to you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thanks. Let me share the slide. Can you see the one that says Calendar Sync v1.4 incident?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yep, I can see it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So I want to start with the incident, because it's the most important thing that happened in engineering this quarter, and I'd rather you hear it from me plainly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On the fifteenth of September we shipped Calendar Sync v1.4, and it introduced a bug. When a technician's Google calendar has a recurring event, and one occurrence of that event has been moved, our sync treated the moved occurrence as a new event and created a duplicate job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Was it only Google calendars? What about Microsoft?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Only Google. Microsoft represents moved occurrences differently in its API, so that path wasn't affected. About seventy percent of our technicians are on Google, though, so that's cold comfort.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: How many jobs are we talking about?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Fernhollow was hit hardest, with about a hundred and thirty duplicate jobs over two weeks. Five other customers had smaller numbers, about forty duplicates between them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Dispatchers were seeing the same job twice, and in a few cases two technicians were sent to the same house.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Ouch. That's a painful one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah, ouch is right. Where we are today, Maya found the root cause. The fix is to dedupe on the iCalUID plus the recurrence ID, and it's in code review now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We're expecting to ship it early next week, together with a cleanup script that removes the existing duplicates.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In the meantime, Tom has been cleaning up duplicates by hand with the affected customers every morning. Which is not a sustainable way to run a company, but it kept the damage contained.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I appreciate the candour. What I care about more than the bug is the process, because bugs happen. What did this tell you about how you build and ship?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Four things, and none of them are flattering. First, we had no test coverage for recurring events with a moved occurrence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The test suite has recurring events, but not exceptions to them, which is exactly what real calendars are full of.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Second, we shipped v1.4 to every customer on the same day. No staged rollout, no feature flag. If we'd rolled it out to ten percent of accounts first, we'd have caught it with a fraction of the damage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Third, we found out from the customer. Owen emailed Tom on the eighteenth, and our monitoring never noticed that one account was suddenly creating twice as many jobs as usual.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And fourth, it landed on one person. Maya was on call for most of the incident while also leading v2. She's exhausted, and that's on me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So what are you changing?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Sync changes now go out behind flags, in stages, starting with our own test accounts and then about ten percent of customers. And we're building a fixture suite of real-world calendar weirdness, moved occurrences, cancelled occurrences, time zone changes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We're adding an alert on job creation rate per account, so a spike pages us before a customer has to email us. And the senior backend hire, which we'll get to, is partly about making on-call a real rotation and not just Maya.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Did any of this breach an SLA? Are you on the hook for credits anywhere?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: No. Our standard contract has an uptime SLA, and the app was up the whole time. There's nothing in the contract about sync accuracy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But I don't take a lot of comfort from that, because the customer doesn't care that the app was up if their technicians are driving to the same house.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And be careful there with Brightkite. Enterprise buyers will want an SLA that covers data correctness, and you need to decide what you can actually stand behind before Lena puts it in a redline.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's fair. It's a good point, and it's not something we've thought through properly yet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: How did the other five customers find out? Did you tell them, or did they discover it?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Honestly, most of them discovered it. We emailed the affected customers once we understood it was systemic, which was around the twenty-first, so three or four days after the first report.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's too slow, and the communication was ad hoc. It was Tom writing individual emails.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Why did it take three or four days to realise it was systemic?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Because the first report looked like a one-off. Tom's first assumption was a configuration problem at Fernhollow, which is usually the right assumption. It was only when a second customer reported the same thing that we pulled the logs across all accounts.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: With the alert we're adding, that cross-account view would have been there on day one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Then I'd push you on a status page. A public, customer-facing one. It sounds like a small thing, but when something breaks, customers mostly want to know that you know.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And enterprise buyers like Brightkite will ask for one. It's usually a line item on the security questionnaire.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I agree, and we don't have one. I'd rather commit to it than talk about it. I'll own getting a customer-facing status page live by the end of October.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'm supportive. Can it be a hosted one, though? I don't want engineering building a status page from scratch.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It'll be a hosted one. I'm not spending any of Maya's time on it, don't worry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And put the incident history on it, not just a green light. A status page that's always green is worse than none, nobody believes it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: End of October. Okay, I'm writing that down.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And I'd like the board to see a proper write-up of the incident. Not the internal postmortem, something short. What happened, what it cost, what you're changing, and how you'll know it worked.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yes. I'll write an incident-review one-pager for the board and send it by Friday the ninth of October. By then the fix will have shipped, so I can include the cleanup numbers too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Perfect, thank you, Shreyas. And give Maya the credit in it, by name. She found it and fixed it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: She will. She's earned it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: One more on process. Was the postmortem blameless? Because if the team thinks it's about who wrote the bug, the next one gets hidden for a day longer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It was, and it will be. The change that caused it was reviewed by two people, and the review checklist didn't have anything about recurring exceptions. That's a process gap, not a person.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Can I ask what this cost you, roughly? Beyond the Fernhollow expansion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Mostly time. Tom has spent maybe sixty percent of the last two weeks on this, and Maya most of hers. Our ticket volume is up about forty percent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And v2 is maybe a week behind where it would have been, but we haven't moved the dates yet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Haven't moved them yet is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It is. If it moves, you'll hear it from me first. Right now the thirteenth of November beta is still the plan.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, the rest of my section. We did Q4 planning yesterday, and we landed on four priorities, in order.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: One is Calendar Sync v2, which we've covered. Two is SOC 2 Type II.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Priya Nair owns it. Our auditor is Kestrel Audit, and the observation window starts on the first of November. It's a three month window, so the report should land in the first quarter of next year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: What's the SOC 2 costing you all in?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Kestrel is about thirty-eight thousand for the Type II, plus around fifteen thousand a year for the compliance tooling. The real cost is Priya, who'll spend maybe a third of her time on it this quarter.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Who's the executive sponsor? Auditors like to see one name at the top.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Me. Priya runs it day to day, but it's my name on it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That's nicely timed with a raise in the spring.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's not an accident. Three is offline mode for the technician mobile app. We cut it for Q4 to a read-only offline job list, so technicians in basements and rural areas can still see their day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Full offline editing moved to Q1. It's a much bigger problem, conflict resolution and all of that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Is offline a deal-breaker for anyone, or a nice to have?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: For the rural customers it's close to a deal-breaker. We have two accounts where technicians spend half the day in crawl spaces or out of coverage, and right now they screenshot their schedule in the morning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's a pretty good argument for doing it, honestly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And four is the new-customer onboarding revamp. Today it takes a new customer about nineteen days to get to their first real dispatch, which is too slow, and it's also a support cost. Noor and Tom are leading it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Nineteen days is long. In my experience the first month decides whether a customer expands or just tolerates you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Agreed. We want it under a week. Noor's running a working session on it later this week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: One thing I'd suggest is measuring it per customer and putting it in front of the board, not just the average. The averages always look better than the worst customer's experience.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's a good idea. Let us think about how to show that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And what did you cut?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Two things. Route optimisation, which customers ask about but which is a huge research project, and the Salesforce integration Aisha mentioned. Both are explicitly out of Q4.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Is cutting Salesforce going to hurt the enterprise deals?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: None of the four enterprise deals has it as a requirement. One mentioned it as a nice to have. We'll revisit in Q1 if that changes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fine, that seems reasonable. Different question, and I have to ask it because every one of my boards gets asked it. What's the AI story?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Honestly, a modest one for now. We prototyped suggesting the best technician for a job, based on skills, location and the calendar, and dispatchers liked it in testing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But it's really a cousin of route optimisation, which we just cut, and I'd rather ship v2 and offline properly than bolt on an AI feature for the deck.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I respect that. Just be ready for it in March, because every Series A investor will ask.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We will. I'd like to have something live in a pilot by then, but not at the cost of the Q4 list.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, fair enough, moving on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, so the two decisions. First, hiring. We'd like approval for two engineering hires, a senior backend engineer and a mobile engineer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Senior backend is about scaling sync and making on-call sustainable. Mobile is offline mode, and frankly Diego is our only mobile engineer, which is a risk in itself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Fully loaded, the two hires together are about forty-five thousand a month. That takes burn from three ten to about three fifty-five, and runway at flat revenue from nineteen months to about seventeen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And how exposed are you on mobile today, with just Diego?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Very. If Diego is on holiday, nobody else can ship a mobile release. That's the main reason the mobile hire matters as much as the backend one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And with the plan revenue?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: With the Q4 plan and a modest 2027 plan, we're comfortably past twenty months, and we'd still have well over twelve months of runway when we start raising in March.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: What are you planning to pay? I don't want you losing the good ones on comp.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The senior backend band is a hundred and seventy to a hundred and ninety base, and mobile is a hundred and fifty to a hundred and sixty-five. Equity is in the range we discussed in July, from the existing pool.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That's in the right range. Don't be afraid to go to the top of it for the right person.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: How confident are you that you can hire them quickly? A senior backend engineer in this market is not a two week process.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We have a strong pipeline for the backend role. There's a candidate in the system design round on Friday who I'm genuinely excited about. Mobile is earlier, but we have a couple of referrals from Diego.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay. Look, I'm supportive. My one condition, which isn't really a condition, is that I want to see the updated model with the hires in it, with Q4 at plan and at, say, seventy percent of plan.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's easy. I'll send you the updated financial model with both scenarios by Friday, so the second of October.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Are you using an agency?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Not for backend, our own pipeline is good. For mobile we might use one if the referrals don't pan out in the next few weeks. A fee of about twenty percent is already in the model.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Then I approve both hires.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I approve as well. I'd much rather you hire engineers now than have Maya burn out in December.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: One request, though. When the backend hire starts, don't throw them straight onto the on-call rotation in week one. Give them a month of shadowing first, or you'll burn out two people instead of one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Agreed. The plan is a month of shadowing, then they join the rotation. Until then, Priya and I take more of the on-call shifts so Maya gets a break.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: You personally on call? That's a CTO doing the right thing, but don't make it permanent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It won't be. It's a bridge until we have enough people for a proper rotation of five.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Great. So both hires are approved. Thank you, both of you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The second decision is fundraising timing. Our recommendation is that we don't start Series A conversations now. We start in March 2027.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: By March we should be at around three million ARR, Calendar Sync v2 will be live, the SOC 2 Type II report will be close or done, and hopefully Brightkite is a logo.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's a much stronger story than today, when the most recent thing a diligent investor finds is an incident.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Have you got a rough size in mind for the A?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Somewhere between twelve and fifteen million, enough for about thirty months. We'll firm it up in January, when we know how Q4 actually landed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: If you had to pick one number to walk into the A with, what is it?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Net new ARR per quarter, with burn multiple next to it. If we can show six hundred thousand a quarter at a burn multiple under one and a half, the rest of the story writes itself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Let me play devil's advocate. The market's decent right now and your numbers are good. There's an argument for opening conversations now, quietly, and seeing if someone pre-empts.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Even a small extension now, a million or two from insiders, would give you a cushion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We talked about it. I don't think we need the cushion with nineteen months, and I don't want to spend the next three months in pitch meetings instead of closing Brightkite. And an extension now would muddy the pricing for the A.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I agree with Aisha. Raising from strength in March is better than raising from okay in October. Daniel, unless you feel strongly?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I don't feel strongly. I'm fine holding until March. I'd only say, don't go completely dark.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Have some coffees, no decks, no asks. When you do start, you want people who already know you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's fair. I'll keep a few relationships warm, but no process until March.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And if it's useful, I might be able to make a couple of introductions in the new year. No promises, let's see where things are.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I'd also think about whether you want a third independent on the board after the A. Not now, but it's worth having a view.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Noted. That's a conversation for after the round.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay. I'm aligned with that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Great. So we hold Series A conversations until March 2027. Anything else from either of you before we wrap?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Just one thing. Shreyas, how is Maya, really? You said she's exhausted, so is she a flight risk?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I don't think she's a flight risk, but I'm watching it. Once the fix ships, I want to take her off the on-call rotation for a couple of weeks. And there's a conversation about her growth that's overdue.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Good. Your best engineer leaving after an incident is a far bigger risk than the incident itself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: One small informational item from me, nothing to decide. Our 409A valuation is due for a refresh, and the firm will reach out to you both in October with a short questionnaire.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: No problem, just send it over when it comes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: One more from me. You mentioned a while ago that you might look at usage-based pricing at some point. Is that still on the table?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It came up, but no, not this year. Forty-five dollars per technician per month on annual contracts, sixty for enterprise with SSO and SCIM. It's simple and it's working, so we're not touching it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fair enough. Maybe something to think about for the A narrative, but not now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, let me read back the actions. I'll send Daniel the updated financial model by Friday the second. Shreyas sends the board the incident one-pager by the ninth.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Ruth, you'll introduce me to the customer success candidate.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Yes. I'll email you directly, Aisha. She's travelling, so it might take her a few days to reply.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And the status page live by the end of October, which is mine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the next board meeting. I was going to propose the fifteenth of December, same time. Does that work for everyone?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The fifteenth of December works for me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Works for me too. Put it in and I'll actually accept it this time, not tentative.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Any big plans before then, Ruth?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: My niece is getting married in Edinburgh this weekend, so mostly I'll be trying to find a hat. Then nothing exciting until Christmas.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'll send the invite today, and I'll include Sam.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Thanks, both. Good quarter, despite the incident. And thanks for being straight about it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thanks, Daniel. Thanks, Ruth. Say hi to Biscuit for us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: He's asleep. As predicted. Bye, everyone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Bye, both. Good luck with Brightkite tomorrow.
